examples.title: Sales by category, SPARQL inside SQL
examples.description: SPASQL: the RDF View is queried in SPARQL and the result is used as a SQL derived table, so SQL tools see ordinary rows.
examples.query:
SELECT categoryName, totalSales, units
FROM (
  SPARQL
  PREFIX nw: <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/Northwind/>
  SELECT ?categoryName
         (ROUND(SUM(?q * ?p * (1 - ?d))) AS ?totalSales)
         (SUM(?q) AS ?units)
  FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/Northwind#>
  WHERE {
    ?od a nw:Order_Details ;
        nw:quantity ?q ; nw:unitprice ?p ; nw:discount ?d ;
        nw:has_products ?product .
    ?product nw:has_categories ?cat .
    ?cat nw:categoryname ?categoryName .
  }
  GROUP BY ?categoryName
  ORDER BY DESC(?totalSales)
) AS x

examples.title: Products in stock, through the RDF View
examples.description: The outer WHERE product IS NOT NULL drops an empty row an RDF View can return under LIMIT.

examples.title: The dashboard post's SalesPerformance query
examples.description: The original SPASQL from the dashboard post (abridged here), opened from the post's own short link. That link predates the presets, so the Query Builder may also ask for the user and password: use demo / demo.
examples.query:
SELECT orderDetail, product, productId, categoryId, orderId,
       categoryName, totalSales, numberOfOrders, totalUnits, avgPrice
FROM (
  SPARQL
  SELECT ?orderDetail ?product ?category ?categoryId ?productId ?orderId ?categoryName
         (ROUND(SUM(?quantity * ?unitPrice * (1 - ?discount))) AS ?totalSales)
         (COUNT(DISTINCT ?orderId) AS ?numberOfOrders)
         (SUM(?quantity) AS ?totalUnits)
         (ROUND(AVG(?unitPrice)) AS ?avgPrice)
  FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/Northwind#>
  WHERE { … Order_Details, Products and Categories … }
  GROUP BY ?categoryName ?orderDetail ?product ?category ?categoryId ?productId ?orderId
  ORDER BY DESC(?totalSales)
) AS SalesPerformance

examples.title: Top customers by sales, SPARQL inside SQL
examples.description: The SQL Server RDF View, aggregated in SPARQL and handed back to SQL as rows.
examples.query:
SELECT company_name, total_quantity, total_sales
FROM (
  SPARQL
  PREFIX ns: <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/northwind-sqlserver/>
  SELECT ?company_name
         (SUM(?quantity) AS ?total_quantity)
         (ROUND(SUM(?quantity * ?unit_price)) AS ?total_sales)
  FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/northwind-sqlserver#>
  WHERE {
    ?customer a ns:customers ; ns:companyname ?company_name .
    ?order a ns:orders ; ns:has_customers ?customer ; ns:orderid ?order_id .
    ?order_detail a ns:order_details ; ns:orderid ?order_id ;
                  ns:unitprice ?unit_price ; ns:quantity ?quantity .
  }
  GROUP BY ?company_name
  ORDER BY DESC(?total_sales)
  LIMIT 10
) AS x

examples.description: A join and an aggregate over two attached Databricks tables. The SPARQL card "Revenue by city" below returns the same numbers through the RDF View.

examples.title: Revenue by city, SPARQL inside SQL
examples.description: The Databricks RDF View, aggregated in SPARQL and handed back to SQL as rows.
examples.query:
SELECT city, orders, revenue
FROM (
  SPARQL
  PREFIX : <http://www.databricks.com/bakehouse#>
  SELECT ?city
         (COUNT(DISTINCT ?transaction) AS ?orders)
         (SUM(?totalPrice) AS ?revenue)
  FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/databricks-bakehouse-r2rml#>
  WHERE {
    ?transaction a :Transaction ;
                 :franchise ?franchise ;
                 :totalPrice ?totalPrice .
    ?franchise :city ?city .
  }
  GROUP BY ?city
  ORDER BY DESC(?revenue)
  LIMIT 10
) AS x

examples.title: The article's databases-per-GB rule, as SQL over SPARQL
examples.description: From the post: SPARQL counts databases per cluster and passes each cluster's hyperlink through as a column; SQL then applies the article's rule of 5 databases per GB of RAM, capped at 100 in preview and 250 at general availability.
examples.query:
SELECT c, cluster_name, ram_gb, dbs,
       ram_gb * 5 AS by_ram,
       CASE WHEN ram_gb * 5 > 100 THEN 100 ELSE ram_gb * 5 END - dbs AS headroom_preview,
       CASE WHEN ram_gb * 5 > 250 THEN 250 ELSE ram_gb * 5 END - dbs AS headroom_ga
FROM (SPARQL
  PREFIX skg: <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/ScaleKG/>
  PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
  SELECT ?c ?cluster_name ?ram_gb (COUNT(?db) AS ?dbs)
  FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/ScaleKG#>
  WHERE {
    ?c a skg:Cluster ; schema:name ?cluster_name ; skg:ramGb ?ram_gb .
    OPTIONAL { ?db skg:hostedOn ?c }
  }
  GROUP BY ?c ?cluster_name ?ram_gb
) AS x
ORDER BY dbs DESC

examples.title: Graph walk joined to a native SQL table
examples.description: From the post: SPARQL walks tenant → owned database in the RDF View, and SQL joins those rows to the analytics_job table to sum billed seconds per tenant, keeping each tenant's hyperlink beside its name.
examples.query:
SELECT t.tenant_iri, t.tenant, COUNT(*) AS jobs, SUM(j.billed_seconds) AS billed_seconds
FROM (SPARQL
  PREFIX skg: <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/ScaleKG/>
  PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
  SELECT ?tenant_iri ?tenant ?db_name
  FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/ScaleKG#>
  WHERE {
    ?tenant_iri a skg:Tenant ; schema:name ?tenant .
    ?db skg:ownedBy ?tenant_iri ; schema:name ?db_name .
  }
) AS t
JOIN ScaleKG.kidehen.graph_database d ON d.db_name = t.db_name
JOIN ScaleKG.kidehen.analytics_job j ON j.db_id = d.db_id
GROUP BY t.tenant_iri, t.tenant
ORDER BY billed_seconds DESC

examples.title: Three hops from tenant to warehouse table
examples.description: Tenant → workload → warehouse table → source, followed as links. The Snowflake tables show up with the workloads that read them.
examples.query:
PREFIX skg: <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/ScaleKG/>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
SELECT ?tenantIri ?tenant ?workloadIri ?workload ?tableIri ?tableName ?source
FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/ScaleKG#>
WHERE {
  ?tenantIri a skg:Tenant ; schema:name ?tenant .
  ?workloadIri skg:forTenant ?tenantIri ; schema:name ?workload ; skg:readsFrom ?tableIri .
  ?tableIri schema:name ?tableName ; skg:inSource ?sourceIri .
  ?sourceIri schema:name ?source .
}
ORDER BY ?tenant ?workload ?tableName

examples.title: Entailment: what is a data asset?
examples.description: With the ScaleKG inference rules on, graph databases and warehouse tables both answer as skg:DataAsset, a class no table declares.
examples.query:
DEFINE input:inference "urn:scalekg:inference"
PREFIX skg: <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/ScaleKG/>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?kindIri ?kind (COUNT(DISTINCT ?assetIri) AS ?assets)
FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/ScaleKG#>
FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/ScaleKG/>
WHERE {
  ?assetIri a skg:DataAsset ; a ?kindIri .
  ?kindIri rdfs:label ?kind .
  FILTER(?kindIri IN (skg:DataAsset, skg:GraphDatabase, skg:WarehouseTable))
}
GROUP BY ?kindIri ?kind
ORDER BY DESC(?assets)

examples.title: The property hierarchy, read from the TBox
examples.description: Joins the ontology graph to find every property declared a sub-property of skg:dependsOn and follows it from each workload.
examples.query:
PREFIX skg: <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/ScaleKG/>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT DISTINCT ?workloadIri ?workload ?relation ?dependencyIri ?dependency
FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/ScaleKG#>
FROM <http://demo.openlinksw.com/schemas/ScaleKG/>
WHERE {
  ?workloadIri a skg:Workload ; schema:name ?workload ; ?relationIri ?dependencyIri .
  ?relationIri rdfs:subPropertyOf skg:dependsOn ; rdfs:label ?relation .
  ?dependencyIri schema:name ?dependency .
}

examples.title: Which SQL table feeds which predicate
examples.description: RDF Views describe themselves: the quad maps are queryable, so you can see the SQL table behind each predicate.
examples.query:
PREFIX virtrdf: <http://www.openlinksw.com/schemas/virtrdf#>
SELECT DISTINCT ?s1 AS ?quadMap ?s3 AS ?rdfPredicate ?s2 AS ?sqlTable
WHERE {
  ?s1 a virtrdf:QuadMap .
  ?s1 virtrdf:qmTableName ?s2 .
  ?s1 virtrdf:qmPredicateRange-rvrFixedValue ?s3 .
  FILTER (! contains(str(?s2), "/csv"))
  FILTER (! contains(str(?s2), 'csv.'))
  FILTER (contains(str(?s2), "supplier"))
}
LIMIT 200

sponger.title: GitHub: the ai-agent-skills repository
sponger.description: The Sponger reads a GitHub repository page into a graph named by the repository URL: page metadata, extracted entities and annotations, and provenance for the load. The query below reads what is already there; Re-sponge sends the full query, which starts with DEFINE get:soft "replace" so the repository page is fetched again first.
sponger.query:
SELECT DISTINCT (?o AS ?EntityType) (SAMPLE(?s) AS ?sampleEntity) (COUNT (*) AS ?EntityCount)
FROM <https://github.com/OpenLinkSoftware/ai-agent-skills>
WHERE {
        ?s a ?o.
}
GROUP BY ?o
ORDER BY DESC (?EntityCount)
sponger.respongeQuery:
DEFINE get:soft "replace"
SELECT DISTINCT (?o AS ?EntityType) (SAMPLE(?s) AS ?sampleEntity) (COUNT (*) AS ?EntityCount)
FROM <https://github.com/OpenLinkSoftware/ai-agent-skills>
WHERE {
        ?s a ?o.
}
GROUP BY ?o
ORDER BY DESC (?EntityCount)

prompts.text: What is a Virtuoso RDF View, and how does it differ from loading data into the quad store?
How do I create an RDF View over a SQL Server table that is attached to Virtuoso?
Which OpenLink drivers connect an application to PostgreSQL over ODBC or JDBC?
How do I attach a PostgreSQL table to Virtuoso through a JDBC data source?
How do I map Databricks tables attached to Virtuoso with R2RML?

faq.q: Does Virtuoso generate an ontology from my database?
faq.a: Yes. Generating an RDF View also generates its ontology: a class for every table, a typed datatype property for every column, and an object property for every foreign key, each with its own IRI and a label naming the SQL source. You can then align those classes with shared ontologies such as FOAF, schema.org or DBpedia, and query every source in the shared terms. The Ontologies page shows both on the live server.

faq.q: Which databases does this work with?
faq.a: Any DBMS that Virtuoso can reach over ODBC or JDBC. Its tables are linked into Virtuoso and can then be exposed through an RDF View, so every row gets its own hyperlink. The showcases on this site use Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Databricks and native Virtuoso SQL tables as examples, plus a synthetic Snowflake-style warehouse estate. The Databricks view is mapped with R2RML, the W3C mapping language, which Virtuoso turns into quad maps.

A mapping, written as quad maps, that presents the tables of any ODBC- or JDBC-accessible DBMS as RDF without copying them. Each row gets a hyperlink of its own that works as a cross-platform super-key, columns become properties and foreign keys become links. SPARQL queries are translated to SQL against the source tables at query time.

faq.q: What does SQL over XMLA mean here?
faq.a: XMLA (XML for Analysis) is a SOAP protocol for sending SQL to a server over HTTP. The SPASQL Query Builder posts your SQL to Virtuoso's /XMLA endpoint with the data source DSN=Local_Instance, so a browser can run SQL without an ODBC driver. Each SQL card can show the request it sends.

SPARQL inside SQL. A SPARQL query is placed in a SQL FROM clause, written FROM (SPARQL …) AS alias, and its result behaves like a derived table. Any SQL client can then use graph data, and SQL can filter or join it further.

faq.q: Why do SQL and SPASQL ask me to sign in?
faq.a: The demo instance is protected by ABAC ACLs. SPARQL is open to anonymous users, while SQL and SPASQL need a session. Sign in with user name demo and password demo, or vdb and vdb. The Query Builder links on this site already preset the demo account for the query itself.

Virtuoso's Linked Data middleware. Cartridges turn web resources such as HTML pages, feeds, repositories and social posts into RDF, stored in a graph named by the source URL. Adding DEFINE get:soft "replace" to a query fetches or refreshes that graph.

faq.q: Why do the Sponger cards run without the DEFINE pragma?
faq.a: Fetching new content needs a signed-in session on URIBurner. The graphs the Sponger has already built can be read by anyone, so the cards query those, and the Re-sponge link adds the pragma for a fresh fetch.

faq.q: How are OPAL agents “loosely coupled” with Data Spaces?
faq.a: An agent holds instructions and a list of query functions, not a copy of the data. At answer time the model picks a function and Virtuoso runs a predefined SQL, SPARQL or SPASQL query against whichever Data Space the function names. You can change the model, the agent or the data without rebuilding the others.

faq.q: Can I put the chat widget on my own site?
faq.a: Yes. Load opal.js and auth.js, then create new Opal(...) with your host, callbacks and an agent module, as the Widget usage section shows. Register your own API key on URIBurner, or sign users in with Solid OIDC.
